entries.text: Lin pressed the tape-deck selector and kept her finger there. Zhou smoothed the faded label, then slid the blank archive form toward her.
The gesture felt like handing over a memory that could finally be named. The microphone lamp went dark, leaving the old reel turning slowly.
Thank you—not because it's my voice, but because it kept this place alive for thirteen more years. I thought that first shift proved only my fear.
Instead, the people who came later heard a station still breathing. I never imagined that was what my frightened voice had carried forward.
Don't trim it. Send the breath at the start, the chair against the wall, and the last half-second of noise.
The archive doesn't need a broadcaster who never made a mistake. It should remember someone carrying morning down the mountain while afraid.
All right; levels are set, and the receiving window is connected. You start the reel; thirteen years ago I thought one slow second would lose the world.
Now I want to watch someone else send that voice for me. When the needle crossed the white line, Lin rested her hand on Play.
The reel quickened, and every repaired join passed cleanly over the head. Old hiss filled the room with the clock and the wind.
The relay also caught two people trying not to breathe too loudly. Zhou watched Lin's hand instead of the meters.
“This is Cape Hill Community Radio. Good morning. May someone hear you today.”
When the receive lamp steadied, Lin printed the temporary receipt while Zhou left the stopped reel on the deck. They climbed the narrow stairs without taking it.
The tape finally seemed to belong to the archive rather than either of them. Above the roof, the eastern clouds had begun to pale.
So this is where we hear those words from the antenna for the last time. Monitor speakers round off every crack.
The wind gives each pause back unchanged. When that breath played downstairs, the younger you no longer seemed trapped inside the tape.
Ten seconds to the master switch now. Watch the status lamp, and tell me only when it is completely dark.
I used to shut the sound off before every sign-off. Today I want to see the last trace of light finish.
An antenna cable swayed in the wind and made a metal sound too small to carry. The old six-point-eight-second call had already left the tower.
Along the archive line, it became a record someone could find again. Only the cable remained, keeping time for a voice that had ended.
Read the receipt once more, please. I need to know the call didn't remain only in our ears or become something polished and unfamiliar.
If the opening breath is registered too, I'll believe they received all of you, not just a clean archival sample.
Received: old station call, six point eight seconds complete, original pauses and room noise retained, marked as Cape Hill Community Radio's final live record.
The notes include your restoration report and my name on duty. They accepted a place where people worked, not a monument.
That's enough. When someone opens it, they will hear your younger breath before the greeting and know that what lasted thirteen years was never a perfect voice.
It was someone sitting down at the microphone again and again. Zhou smiled and did not correct Lin for saying “we” as “you.”
Only after Lin said “dark” did Zhou press the master switch. The red lamp faded, and the tower's last low hum sank into the wind.
He gave Lin the key without turning back to check. The city below entered morning quietly, while the old tape had somewhere new to go.
The Old Voice, Archived
